n: Six days after Peter’s confession, Jesus takes his three closest apostles up a high mountain. The same three will later be with him in Gethsemane.

f.g: Traditionally Mount Tabor; many scholars suggest Mount Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi.

n: Jesus is transfigured — his divine glory shines through. His face blazes like the sun and his clothing becomes brilliant white.

f.g: Greek metamorphoō — changed in form or appearance.
raiment = clothing.

n: Moses (representing the law) and Elijah (representing the prophets) appear and speak with Jesus — Luke says about his coming death in Jerusalem.

f.g: Elias = Elijah. Latter-day Saints believe these two conferred priesthood keys on Peter, James, and John here, as they later did in the Kirtland Temple.

n: Overwhelmed, Peter offers to build three shelters. He wants to hold on to this glorious moment.

f.g: Booths or tents, like those used at the Feast of Tabernacles.

n: A bright cloud — a sign of God’s presence — surrounds them, and the Father’s voice declares Jesus his beloved Son, as at his baptism, adding “hear ye him.”
Hearing God’s voice, the apostles fall face down in awe and fear.

f.g: sore = greatly, intensely.

n: Jesus gently touches them and tells them to get up and not be afraid.
When they look up, only Jesus remains. The law and the prophets give way to him alone.

f.g: save = except.

n: Coming down, Jesus tells them to keep the vision secret until after his resurrection, when it could be properly understood.

f.w: Tell the vision to no man

n: Having just seen Elijah, the disciples ask about the scribes’ teaching that Elijah must come before the Messiah.
Jesus affirms that Elijah will indeed come and restore all things — a prophecy Latter-day Saints see fulfilled in part in 1836.
Yet in another sense Elias had already come in John the Baptist, and he was rejected and killed. Jesus would suffer the same.

f.g: listed = wished, pleased.

n: The disciples realize he means John the Baptist, the forerunner who came in the spirit and power of Elijah.
Back at the foot of the mountain, a desperate father kneels before Jesus.
His son suffers violent seizures that throw him into fire and water. Mark describes the cause as an evil spirit.

f.g: Greek selēniazomai — literally “moonstruck”; it described seizures, which people then linked to the moon.
Severely tormented.

n: The disciples left behind had tried and failed to heal the boy.
Jesus expresses sorrow at the faithlessness he finds, then asks for the boy to be brought to him.

f.g: Twisted, turned from the right way.
suffer = bear with, put up with.

n: Jesus rebukes the evil spirit, and the boy is healed at once.
Privately, the disciples ask why their attempt failed.

f.g: Privately, away from the crowd.

n: Their faith was too weak. Even faith as small as a mustard seed, if genuine and growing, can move mountains.

f.w: faith as a grain of mustard seed

n: Some challenges require the extra spiritual power that comes through prayer and fasting.

f.g: Some ancient manuscripts lack this verse; Mark 9:29 contains the same teaching.
howbeit = however.

n: In Galilee, Jesus again predicts that he will be betrayed into human hands.

f.g: Greek paradidōmi — handed over, delivered up.

n: He foretells his death and resurrection on the third day. The disciples are deeply grieved, hearing the death more clearly than the rising.

f.w: the third day he shall be raised again

n: In Capernaum, collectors of the annual temple tax ask Peter whether Jesus pays it.

f.g: The half-shekel temple tax every Jewish man paid yearly for the temple’s upkeep.

n: Peter says yes. Before Peter can mention it, Jesus raises the question: do kings tax their own sons or others?

f.g: prevented = went before him, spoke first.
custom = duties, tolls.

n: Kings tax outsiders, not their own children. As God’s Son, Jesus owes no tax to his Father’s house.
Still, to avoid giving needless offense, Jesus sends Peter fishing. The first fish holds a coin worth exactly the tax for both of them.

f.g: Greek statēr — a coin worth four drachmas, exactly two half-shekel taxes.
